entities.name: Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologos dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologos dynasty (1261-1453 CE), the longest-ruling Byzantine dynasty and the last, governed Byzantium from its recovery of Constantinople (from the Latin Empire in 1261) through its final, inexorable decline and the Ottoman conquest of 1453. The Palaiologan restoration — achieved by Michael VIII Palaiologos's recapture of Constantinople on July 25, 1261 — began with genuine optimism, but the empire Michael recovered was a shadow of the pre-1204 Byzantium: stripped of most territory, exhausted financially, and facing both the Ottomans in the east and the Venetians in commerce.

The dynasty's defining tragedy is the contrast between cultural flourishing and political decline. The Palaiologan Renaissance (13th-15th centuries) produced Theodore Metochites, Gregory Palamas, Gemistos Plethon, and Constantine Laskaris — Byzantine scholars whose Greek manuscripts, carried to Italy (especially after 1453), directly fueled the Italian Renaissance. The Chora Church's mosaics (c. 1316) are perhaps the most beautiful Byzantine art surviving. Yet simultaneously, the civil wars between John V and John VI (1341-1354) invited Ottoman intervention: it was during these civil wars that Ottoman forces first crossed into Europe (1354, Gallipoli).

Constantine XI Palaiologos, the dynasty's last emperor, died fighting on the walls of Constantinople on May 29, 1453, as Ottoman cannon breached the Theodosian Walls. His death ended 1,123 years of Eastern Roman history. The Greek scholars who fled to Italy before and after 1453 brought their manuscripts of Plato, Aristotle, and Greek scientific texts — directly catalyzing the Italian Renaissance and the recovery of classical learning that produced the Scientific Revolution.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Palaiologos dynasty — governing Byzantium's last 192 years, ending in the 1453 Ottoman conquest that closed the ancient world, and inadvertently catalyzing the Italian Renaissance through its fleeing scholars — is one of history's most consequential dynasties: its end launched the modern era.
